items.stem: Northgate Foods is training new accounting staff on the conceptual framework for financial reporting. Which of the following is a fundamental qualitative characteristic of useful financial information?
options: Comparability
Verifiability
Timeliness
Faithful representation
items.rule_line: Fundamental qualitative characteristics are relevance and faithful representation; comparability, verifiability, timeliness and understandability only enhance them.

why.A: Comparability is an enhancing characteristic. It improves usefulness only after the fundamental characteristics are met.
why.B: Verifiability is an enhancing characteristic, not a fundamental one.
why.C: Timeliness is an enhancing characteristic; it does not by itself make information useful.
why.D: Correct. The two fundamental qualitative characteristics are relevance and faithful representation.

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC/GASB text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: Which two characteristics does the framework label as the fundamental ones?
guide.reveal: Relevance and one that concerns whether the information depicts what it claims to depict.

guide.ask: Of the candidates listed, which one is the second of those two?
guide.reveal: Faithful representation; the others are enhancing characteristics.

items.stem: The owner of Ridgeline Bakery, Inc. paid a personal family vacation from the company checking account and recorded it as office expense. Which basic accounting assumption does this treatment violate?
options: Going concern assumption
Periodicity assumption
Monetary unit assumption
Economic entity assumption
items.rule_line: The economic entity assumption keeps an entity's transactions separate from those of its owners and other entities.

why.A: Going concern concerns whether the entity will continue operating; it says nothing about separating owner and business.
why.B: Periodicity divides the entity's life into reporting periods; the vacation cost does not misstate a period boundary.
why.C: The monetary unit assumption is that transactions are measured in a stable currency, which is not at issue here.
why.D: Correct. The business must be accounted for separately from its owner's personal affairs, so personal spending is not a company expense.

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC/GASB text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: What is the owner's personal spending doing inside the company's books?
guide.reveal: Mixing the owner's private affairs with the business's records.

guide.ask: Which basic assumption requires the business to be kept separate from its owner?
guide.reveal: The economic entity assumption.

items.stem: Cedar Point Manufacturing sold a parcel of land that it had held for future use, for $40,000 more than its carrying amount. Which characterization is most consistent with the conceptual framework?
options: Revenue, because the sale increased net assets during the period
Other comprehensive income, because the sale was not part of operations
A reduction of expense, because the proceeds exceeded the carrying amount
A gain, because it results from a peripheral or incidental transaction
items.rule_line: Gains are increases in net assets from peripheral or incidental transactions; revenues come from ongoing major or central operations.

why.A: Revenue arises from an entity's ongoing major or central operations. Selling idle land is incidental, so the increase is a gain.
why.B: OCI is limited to items the standards specifically direct to OCI. A realized gain on land is recognized in net income.
why.C: The excess of proceeds over carrying amount is not a recovery of a prior cost; it is a separate gain.
why.D: Correct. Increases in net assets from peripheral or incidental transactions are gains; they are reported in net income here because the land is not available-for-sale debt.

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC/GASB text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: Was the land sale part of Cedar Point's central, ongoing operations?
guide.reveal: No, it was a one-time disposal of an asset held for future use.

guide.ask: What does the framework call a net increase from a peripheral or incidental transaction?
guide.reveal: A gain, reported in net income here.

items.stem: Glenrock Technologies, a public company, will issue its financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2026 on March 10, 2027. Management is evaluating whether conditions raise substantial doubt about the entity's ability to continue as a going concern. Through what date must management's evaluation look forward?
options: December 31, 2027
December 31, 2028
March 10, 2027
March 10, 2028
items.rule_line: Management evaluates going concern for one year after the date the financial statements are issued or available to be issued.

why.A: One year after the balance sheet date is the old auditor-style horizon. The horizon runs from the issuance date, not the balance sheet date.
why.B: This is one year after the end of the next fiscal year, which extends the horizon beyond the required period.
why.C: This is the issuance date itself. The evaluation looks forward one year from that date.
why.D: Correct. The evaluation covers one year after the date the financial statements are issued (or available to be issued).

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC/GASB text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: Management's going concern evaluation looks forward from which reference point, the balance sheet date or the issuance date?
guide.reveal: From the date the statements are issued or available to be issued.

guide.ask: How far past that date must the evaluation extend, and what date results?
guide.reveal: One year, so March 10, 2028.

items.stem: At December 31, 2026, Bayfront Marine had recurring operating losses and a $2.4 million loan maturing in June 2027 that it cannot repay from existing resources. Management's only plan is to sell a vessel to a buyer not yet identified, and the plan is not probable of being effectively implemented. Which disclosure is required in the notes?
options: The principal conditions and management's plans only, because the words 'substantial doubt' are reserved for the auditor's report
The principal conditions and a statement that management's plans have alleviated the substantial doubt about continuing as a going concern
No note disclosure, because a going concern assessment is required only in the auditor's report and management letter
The principal conditions, management's evaluation and plans, and a statement that substantial doubt exists about the ability to continue as a going concern
items.rule_line: If plans do not alleviate substantial doubt, disclose the conditions, evaluation, plans and an explicit substantial-doubt statement.

why.A: Management's own disclosure must include the substantial doubt statement. The auditor's report is a separate communication.
why.B: Plans alleviate doubt only when it is probable they will be effectively implemented and will mitigate the conditions. Neither is true here.
why.C: GAAP requires management to evaluate and disclose; the disclosure is not left to the auditor.
why.D: Correct. When plans do not alleviate the doubt, the notes must state that substantial doubt exists in addition to describing conditions, evaluation and plans.

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC/GASB text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: Do management's plans alleviate the doubt in this case?
guide.reveal: No, the plan is not probable of being effectively implemented.

guide.ask: Given that, what must the notes say besides the conditions and plans?
guide.reveal: A statement that substantial doubt exists, along with management's evaluation.

items.stem: Riverbend Co. will issue its December 31, 2026 financial statements on March 5, 2027. Its liabilities at year-end include accounts payable of $250,000, accrued wages of $40,000, current maturities of long-term debt of $100,000, and dividends payable of $30,000. It also has a $600,000 note payable due February 15, 2027. On January 20, 2027, Riverbend issued $700,000 of five-year bonds and used the proceeds to repay the note when due. What amount should Riverbend report as total current liabilities at December 31, 2026?
items.rule_line: A short-term obligation is noncurrent if, before the statements are issued, it is refinanced by issuing long-term debt or equity.

why.A: Omits the $100,000 current maturities of long-term debt, which are due within the next year and remain current.
why.B: Omits the $30,000 dividends payable. Declared dividends are a current liability.
why.C: Correct. The note is excluded because long-term financing was completed before the statements were issued: $250,000 + $40,000 + $100,000 + $30,000 = $420,000.
why.D: Includes the $600,000 note. A short-term obligation refinanced on a long-term basis before issuance of the statements is classified as noncurrent.

steps: Current items: AP 250000 + wages 40000 + current maturities 100000 + dividends 30000 = 420000
Note refinanced with bonds issued Jan 20, 2027 (before Mar 5, 2027 issuance): noncurrent, excluded

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC/GASB text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: Which listed liabilities are ordinary current items?
guide.reveal: Accounts payable, accrued wages, current maturities and dividends payable.

guide.ask: The $600,000 note is due within a year; was long-term refinancing completed before issuance?
guide.reveal: Yes, bonds were issued on January 20 before March 5, so the note is excluded.

guide.ask: What is the sum of the ordinary items?

items.stem: Harlow Corp. had these balances at December 31, 2026: cash $80,000; cash restricted for a plant expansion to be built in 2028, $50,000; accounts receivable $210,000 with an allowance for credit losses of $10,000; inventory $150,000; prepaid insurance $45,000 covering the next 18 months, of which $30,000 will be used up within 12 months of the balance sheet date and $15,000 after that; trading securities $40,000; and an equity-method investment in an affiliate, $90,000. What amount should Harlow report as total current assets?
items.rule_line: Current assets are those expected to be realized or used within one year or the operating cycle; restricted cash for long-term uses is not current.

why.A: Correct. $80,000 + net receivables $200,000 + inventory $150,000 + prepaid insurance for 12 of 18 months $30,000 + trading securities $40,000 = $500,000.
why.B: Treats the whole $45,000 of prepaid insurance as current. Only the portion expiring within the next 12 months is current.
why.C: Includes the $50,000 of restricted cash. Cash restricted for a noncurrent purpose is a noncurrent asset.
why.D: Includes the $90,000 equity-method investment. It is a long-term investment, not a current asset.

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC/GASB text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.reveal: Unrestricted cash 80,000 and receivables net 210,000 - 10,000 = 200,000.

guide.reveal: 12/18 of 45,000 = 30,000 is current; the restricted cash for 2028 and the equity-method investment are noncurrent.

items.stem: On July 1, 2026, Sable Analytics received $1,200,000 for a 24-month software subscription that began that day. Revenue is recognized evenly over the term. What amount should Sable report as a noncurrent contract liability (deferred revenue) at December 31, 2026?
items.rule_line: Split a contract liability into the portion recognized within 12 months (current) and the remainder (noncurrent).

why.A: Correct. Six months (through Dec 31, 2026) is recognized; 18 months remain. The next 12 months ($600,000) are current, so $300,000 is noncurrent.
why.B: This is the current portion for the next 12 months, not the noncurrent portion.
why.C: This is the entire remaining contract liability (18 of 24 months). Part of it is current.
why.D: This is the full amount received, ignoring the six months already earned.

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC/GASB text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: How much revenue is recognized per month?
How much remains unearned at December 31 after six months?
How much of that is due within the next 12 months, and what is left as noncurrent?
guide.reveal: 600,000 is current, so 900,000 - 600,000 = 300,000 is noncurrent.

items.stem: Marlow Inc. operates in a single tax jurisdiction. At December 31, 2026 it has deferred tax assets of $40,000 (from an accrued warranty liability, a current-type item) and deferred tax liabilities of $100,000 (from accelerated depreciation). How should Marlow present these amounts on its classified balance sheet?
options: A current deferred tax asset of $40,000 and a noncurrent deferred tax liability of $100,000
A current deferred tax liability of $60,000
A noncurrent deferred tax asset of $40,000 and a noncurrent deferred tax liability of $100,000, shown separately
A single noncurrent deferred tax liability of $60,000
items.rule_line: All deferred tax balances are noncurrent, and those of the same tax-paying component and jurisdiction are netted.

why.A: Classification by the related asset or liability was eliminated. All deferred taxes are noncurrent and same-jurisdiction amounts are netted.
why.B: The net amount is a noncurrent liability; no deferred tax amount is classified as current.
why.C: They are noncurrent, but same-jurisdiction assets and liabilities must be offset and shown as one net amount.
why.D: Correct. Deferred tax assets and liabilities of the same jurisdiction are netted and classified as noncurrent.

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC/GASB text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: Do deferred tax assets and liabilities of one jurisdiction stay separate or get combined?
guide.reveal: They are netted, since they relate to the same taxing authority.

guide.ask: How are net deferred taxes classified, and what is the net amount?
guide.reveal: Noncurrent; 100,000 - 40,000 = 60,000 net liability.

items.stem: At December 31, 2026, Larkin Corp. had a checking account with a balance of $85,000 at First Bank and an overdraft of $20,000 in a separate account at Second Bank. Larkin has no right of offset between the two banks. What amount should Larkin report as cash in current assets?
items.rule_line: Overdrafts are reported as liabilities and offset against positive balances only for accounts at the same bank with a right of offset.

why.A: Reports only the overdraft amount, which is a liability rather than cash.
why.B: Nets the overdraft against the positive balance. Offsetting is allowed only for accounts at the same bank with a right of offset.
why.C: Correct. The $20,000 overdraft is reported as a current liability because it is at a different bank, so cash stays $85,000.
why.D: Adds the overdraft to cash. An overdraft never increases the cash asset.

steps: Cash = 85000; overdraft 20000 reported separately as a current liability

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC/GASB text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: Can the Second Bank overdraft be offset against the First Bank balance?
guide.reveal: No, there is no right of offset between different banks.

guide.ask: Where does the overdraft go, and what stays in cash?
guide.reveal: It is a current liability; cash remains 85,000.

items.stem: Which of the following must be included in a company's summary of significant accounting policies?
options: The balance of each customer account included in accounts receivable, broken out by customer
The dates and amounts of every journal entry that adjusted the trial balance at year-end
A forecast of next year's revenue and net income prepared by management
The cost-flow assumption used to value inventory, when more than one acceptable method exists
items.rule_line: Disclose accounting policies that management selected from acceptable alternatives, including industry-specific and unusual applications.

why.A: Account-level detail is not a policy disclosure; policies describe the methods used, not individual balances.
why.B: Journal entries are internal records, not policy disclosures.
why.C: Forecasts are not part of the basic financial statements or the policy note.
why.D: Correct. Policies that management selected from acceptable alternatives (for example, inventory methods) must be disclosed.

guide.ask: Which disclosures are the summary of significant accounting policies meant to explain?
guide.reveal: Policies management picked where acceptable alternatives exist.

guide.ask: Which listed item is such a selected policy?
guide.reveal: The inventory cost-flow assumption when several methods are acceptable.

items.stem: At December 31, 2026, Quarry Hill Co. violated a covenant on its $3 million term loan due in 2031, making the loan callable by the lender. Before issuing its statements on March 1, 2027, Quarry Hill obtained a written waiver from the lender covering the violation and waiving the lender's right to demand repayment for 15 months from December 31, 2026. How should the loan be classified at December 31, 2026?
options: Current, because the covenant was violated at the balance sheet date and the loan was therefore callable then
Current, because the waiver period ends only 3 months after the next fiscal year begins
Noncurrent, but only if the violation is also cured by the end of the year following the balance sheet date
Noncurrent, because the lender waived the right to demand repayment for more than one year from the balance sheet date
items.rule_line: A covenant-violating loan stays noncurrent only if the lender waives its right to call it for over one year from the balance sheet date.

why.A: The waiver obtained before issuance, covering more than one year, removes the current classification.
why.B: A waiver longer than one year from the balance sheet date is sufficient; its end date within the next year is irrelevant.
why.C: A waiver for more than one year is sufficient on its own; cure is an alternative route, not an additional requirement.
why.D: Correct. A callable obligation is noncurrent only if the creditor has waived or lost the right to demand repayment for more than one year from the balance sheet date.

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC/GASB text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: Was the covenant violation waived, and for how long from the balance sheet date?
guide.reveal: Yes, in writing before issuance, for 15 months from December 31, 2026.

guide.ask: When is a callable debt still noncurrent?
guide.reveal: When the creditor has waived the right to demand repayment for more than one year from the balance sheet date, which 15 months exceeds.

items.stem: Fenwick Corp.'s board voted in December 2026 to buy a new machine in March 2027 for $500,000 on credit. No purchase order has been signed and no goods were received. Under the conceptual framework, how should Fenwick treat the plan at December 31, 2026?
options: Recognize a liability of $500,000, because the board's vote is a probable future sacrifice of economic benefits
Recognize an asset of $500,000, because the board has committed the entity to control the machine's benefits
Recognize an appropriation of retained earnings of $500,000, because the board has designated resources for it
Do not recognize a liability, because no past transaction or event has created a present obligation to transfer assets
items.rule_line: A liability is a present obligation to transfer assets, arising from past transactions or events; management intentions alone do not create one.

why.A: A probable future sacrifice is only one part of the definition; the obligation must also be present and arise from a past event.
why.B: No asset exists until the entity obtains control of the machine's future benefits through a past transaction.
why.C: Board designations do not create a liability or a reduction of equity in the financial statements.
why.D: Correct. A liability requires a present obligation arising from past transactions or events; a planned future purchase is not one.

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC/GASB text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: Has any transaction or event already occurred that obligates Fenwick to pay?
guide.reveal: No, there is no signed order and no goods received.

guide.ask: What does the definition of a liability require, and does this plan meet it?
guide.reveal: A present obligation from a past event; it does not, so nothing is recognized.

items.stem: For 2026, Tamarack Products reported: gross sales $900,000; sales returns $30,000; sales discounts $20,000; cost of goods sold $510,000; selling and administrative expenses $140,000; interest expense $25,000; interest income $5,000; loss on sale of equipment $12,000; and a $18,000 gain from an insurance recovery after a hurricane, an event that was unusual and infrequent. Tamarack also had a $35,000 loss, net of tax, from a discontinued component. What amount should Tamarack report as income from continuing operations before income taxes?
items.rule_line: Unusual or infrequent items remain in income from continuing operations; discontinued operations are shown separately below, net of tax.

why.A: Deducts the $35,000 discontinued-operations loss. That loss is presented separately after continuing operations, net of tax.
why.B: Excludes the $18,000 hurricane gain as if it were an extraordinary item. Extraordinary-item presentation was eliminated; unusual or infrequent items stay in continuing operations.
why.C: Correct. Net sales $850,000 less cost of goods sold, expenses, interest and the equipment loss, plus interest income and the unusual gain, gives $186,000.
why.D: Adds the $35,000 discontinued-operations loss. It is presented separately, and it is a loss, not an addition.

steps: Less interest expense 25000, plus interest income 5000, less equipment loss 12000, plus hurricane gain 18000: 186000

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC/GASB text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: What is net sales?
After cost of goods sold and selling and administrative expenses, what is left?
Which other items stay in continuing operations, and which is excluded?
guide.reveal: Interest, the equipment loss and the unusual gain all stay; only the discontinued component is excluded. Result 200,000 - 25,000 + 5,000 - 12,000 + 18,000 = 186,000.

items.stem: In 2026, the board of Fairbank Industries committed to sell its wholesale division, a strategic shift that qualifies for discontinued operations reporting. Through the disposal date the division earned pretax income of $180,000, and the disposal produced a pretax loss of $60,000. Fairbank's income tax rate is 30%. What amount should be reported in the income statement as income from discontinued operations, net of tax?
items.rule_line: Report the disposal component's operating results and disposal gain or loss together, net of tax, below continuing operations.

why.A: Correct. Operating income $180,000 less the disposal loss $60,000 is $120,000 pretax; after 30% tax it is $84,000.
why.B: Reports the combined result before tax ($120,000). Discontinued operations are presented net of tax.
why.C: Includes only the operating income after tax ($126,000) and omits the loss on disposal, which is part of discontinued operations.
why.D: Adds the disposal loss to operating income. A loss reduces the result.

guide.reveal: Yes, both belong in discontinued operations, before tax.

items.stem: During 2026, four companies disposed of businesses. Which disposal most clearly qualifies for presentation as a discontinued operation?
options: Quill Retail closed one of its 240 stores, which generated less than 1% of revenue and profit, because the lease expired
Dunmore Foods sold one production line at its main plant and replaced it with a newer line producing the same products
Ashby Co. sold its headquarters building and moved into leased space, continuing all of its lines of business unchanged
Ellery Corp. sold its entire European division, which produced 35% of consolidated revenue, ending its strategy of operating outside North America
items.rule_line: A discontinued operation is a component disposal that represents a strategic shift with a major effect on the entity's operations and financial results.

why.A: A single small store is not a strategic shift and has no major effect on results.
why.B: Replacing equipment within the same business is not a strategic shift or disposal of a component.
why.C: Selling an asset while continuing the business does not dispose of a component.
why.D: Correct. The disposal of a component that represents a strategic shift with a major effect on operations and results qualifies.

verify.cite_ok: unchecked (ASC/GASB text not opened; refs from memory)

guide.ask: Which situations are just routine replacements or small closures with no major effect?
guide.reveal: A single store, a single production line and a headquarters move.

guide.ask: Which disposal ends a whole line of business with a large share of revenue and a strategic shift?
guide.reveal: The sale of the entire European division producing 35% of revenue.

items.stem: At December 31, 2026, Westmere Co. classified a disposal group as held for sale. Its carrying amount was $900,000, its fair value was $780,000, and estimated costs to sell were $40,000. What loss should Westmere recognize at December 31, 2026?
items.rule_line: Held-for-sale assets are measured at the lower of carrying amount or fair value less costs to sell; write-downs are losses.

why.A: Recognizes only the $40,000 of selling costs and ignores the decline from carrying amount to fair value.
why.B: Adds the costs to sell to fair value instead of subtracting them.
why.C: Uses fair value alone ($120,000); costs to sell must also be deducted.
why.D: Correct. Held-for-sale assets are measured at the lower of carrying amount or fair value less costs to sell: $900,000 - ($780,000 - $40,000) = $160,000.

steps: Fair value less costs to sell 780000 - 40000 = 740000

items.stem: Coldwater Shipping is located in a region with no history of tornadoes. In 2026 a tornado destroyed a warehouse, causing an uninsured pretax loss of $2 million; neither the event nor its type is expected to recur. How should Coldwater present the loss?
options: As a separate component of income from continuing operations, before income taxes, or in the notes
As an extraordinary item, net of tax, below income from continuing operations
As a loss from discontinued operations, net of tax, because it will not recur
As a direct charge to retained earnings, because it is outside the normal operations of the entity
items.rule_line: Unusual or infrequent items are presented as a separate component of income from continuing operations, not as extraordinary items.

why.A: Correct. Items that are unusual or infrequent are reported within income from continuing operations and separately identified.
why.B: The extraordinary item category was eliminated by ASU 2015-01. Such items stay in continuing operations.
why.C: Discontinued operations relate to the disposal of a component, not to an isolated casualty loss.

items.stem: Ivory Products reported net income of $120,000 on sales of $1,500,000. Average total assets were $1,000,000 and average stockholders' equity was $400,000. What is return on equity?
items.rule_line: ROE = profit margin x asset turnover x equity multiplier = net income / average equity.

why.A: Multiplies return on assets by the inverse of the equity multiplier, which reduces rather than raises the return.
why.B: Reports only the net profit margin (8.0%).
why.C: Reports return on assets (12.0%), which omits financial leverage.
why.D: Correct. Margin 8.0% x asset turnover 1.5 x equity multiplier 2.5 = 30.0%; equivalently $120,000 / $400,000.

items.stem: Juniper Inc.'s return on equity rose from 15% to 18%. Over the same period its net profit margin fell from 6.0% to 5.0%, and its asset turnover rose from 1.50 to 1.60. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The increase came from higher financial leverage, which more than offset the lower margin
The increase came from improved profitability, because the higher asset turnover raised the net profit margin
The increase came from better asset utilization alone, because turnover rose while leverage stayed constant
The increase came from higher profit margins, because margin and turnover both affect return on equity
items.rule_line: ROE = margin x turnover x leverage; solve the implied equity multiplier to identify the driver of a change.

why.A: Correct. The equity multiplier rose from about 1.67 to 2.25, raising ROE despite the lower margin and modestly better turnover.
why.B: The margin actually fell; turnover is a separate driver.
why.C: Turnover rose only about 7%, not enough; leverage rose about 35%.
why.D: The profit margin declined.

items.stem: Over two years, Nolan Co.'s receivables turnover fell from 9.0 to 6.5, its inventory turnover rose from 5.0 to 7.0, and its gross margin percentage was unchanged. Which explanation is most consistent with these trends?
options: Credit terms were tightened and collections accelerated, while inventory levels grew relative to sales
Both working capital accounts became more efficient, which is why gross margin stayed the same
Credit terms were loosened or collections slowed, while inventory management became tighter
Both working capital accounts became less efficient, offset by an increase in sales prices
items.rule_line: Lower receivables turnover means slower collection; higher inventory turnover means inventory is moving faster.

why.A: Both signals point the opposite way: receivables slowed and inventory speeded up.
why.B: Receivables turnover fell, which is less efficient.
why.C: Correct. Lower receivables turnover signals slower collections; higher inventory turnover signals faster movement of goods.
why.D: Inventory turnover rose, which is more efficient, and prices would change gross margin.

items.stem: Pinnacle Co. reported net income of $200,000, interest expense of $40,000, an income tax rate of 25%, and average total assets of $2,000,000 (ending assets $2,200,000). Using return on assets defined as net income plus after-tax interest, divided by average total assets, what is the ratio?
items.rule_line: ROA = (net income + interest expense x (1 - tax rate)) / average total assets.

why.A: Uses net income only, without adding back after-tax interest (10.0%).
why.B: Uses ending assets instead of average assets (10.5%).
why.D: Adds back interest before tax (12.0%), although interest expense saved a tax deduction.

items.rule_line: Horizontal analysis measures the percentage change in a line item from a base period; here operating income fell 25%.

why.B: Reports the 15.0% growth in revenue, not in operating income.
why.C: Reports the 19.4% growth in expenses, not in operating income.
why.D: Reports the size of the change (25.0%) with the wrong sign; operating income declined.
